subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning a treasure chest module with a root "chest" joint and a hinged "lid" joint, sketching out rough dimensions like a 0.9 width and 0.55 depth for the base.

For the lid, I'm working out the hinge rotation math so it swings open roughly 110° backward and upward from its closed position, binding the lid parts explicitly to the hinge joint and setting its rotation axis along X in model space.

Building the lid geometry now: a box base topped with a half-cylinder barrel shape, scaled and positioned to sit correctly above the hinge point...

Switching approach: instead of an open cylinder shell for the lid, I'll build it as a solid extrusion of a half-ellipse profile so the inner face is visible when open, with the thickness and outline points defining its curved shape.

I'm placing the closed lid at the hinge point, letting its flat bottom face serve as the visible interior when opened, and adding a thin red lining box positioned just inside that face with its own offset and color so it reads correctly in both open and closed poses. Now I'm starting on the chest body itself as a hollow box with a floor and four walls, filled inside with gold.

Building individual plank boxes for the walls...

Now I'm working on the iron straps for the lid, planning arcs along an elliptical path wrapping over the top and sweeping a thin box-section profile outward from the surface.

Next I'm extending straps down onto the body front, adding L-shaped corner straps and horizontal rim bands at top and bottom, then placing small spherical studs along the strap positions manually since I'll need the lid bone for correct placement.

Now I'm picking the rust and dark iron color palette, then designing the hasp and padlock: a plate at the lid front edge connecting to a plate on the body front, with a padlock body and shackle hanging loosely from the staple, slightly tilted.

For the carved skull decoration, I'm deciding on a pale bone-tinted tone with dark outlines so it reads as a carved, worn-paint design against the front planks, placing it as a textured plane just in front of the body wall surface, centered at a modest size.

Now I'm checking placements so the hasp, straps, skull, and hanging lock don't overlap — shrinking the skull slightly and shifting its center, then adjusting the lock's shackle and body position so it hangs tilted and offset to the side below the hasp staple without colliding with the skull art.

For the interior, I'm planning a gold mound made from a squashed sphere sized to fit the chest's inner bounds, positioned so its top spills slightly over the front lip, with some coins scattered on the floor near the front to suggest overflow.

For the coins, I'll generate many small low-sided cylinders in two gold tones, merged by color using BufferGeometryUtils to keep the part count manageable, scattering them randomly across the mound's surface and floor with positions derived from a dummy object's transform matrix.

The mound coins will follow an ellipsoid-shaped height field so they sit naturally on the pile, while spilled coins on the floor in front will thin out with distance, mostly lying flat with a few tilted, plus a separate flattened low pile near the chest's front edge for extra visual mass.

I'll shift that gold blob to avoid covering the skull, repositioning it off-center so it reads as a slope spilling from the rim down to the floor pile without overlapping the skull's visible side.

Coins should orient along the ellipsoid's surface normal using my own aim() helper to build a quaternion, composed into a transform matrix. The main mound is a scaled gold sphere with coins scattered on top, and I'm planning a pearl necklace draped over the front-left rim using a catmull path hanging down the chest's front face.

I'm plotting the necklace's control points — starting inside the chest, over the rim at its top edge, cascading down the front, then looping on the floor — with pearls placed along this path using small spheres oriented to follow the path's frame, while checking whether it might collide with the strap near x=0.28.

Since the necklace clashes with the strap, I'm shifting it inward to x=-0.19, keeping it between the skull and strap on the front face, and rechecking clearance against the strap's outer edge. For bone weighting, I decide to just assign the necklace to the root joint directly, defining a simple root joint at the origin rather than trying to compute nearest-bone distances.

Now I'm setting up a helper function to place parts relative to either the base or lid bone, picking pearl color, estimating pearl count along the necklace path by dividing path length by pearl diameter, and sketching the goblet placement on the chest mound.

Defining the goblet lathe profile...

I'll keep the goblet upright, computing its base height from the mound's curved surface near that position and placing gem decorations (ruby and emerald icosahedrons) in a ring around the cup. Now I'm moving on to placing loose gems scattered separately.

Adding a few scattered red and green gems across the coin pile and floor using small octahedron/dodecahedron shapes with flat shading, plus one larger stretched gem for variety. I'm also adding side iron handles made from a small plate and a torus ring rotated to sit flush against the goblet's sides.

For the back of the chest, I'm placing hinge plates on both the base and lid with a connecting barrel cylinder along the x-axis to simulate the hinge joint.

I also need a floor plank for the chest bottom and a thin rim band around the base and top edges. For the lid's open position, I'm calculating how the lid profile rotates about the hinge when opened 110 degrees, working out the transformed coordinates for the back top point to determine the swing extent.

Checking the front edge gives a world position that confirms the lid leans back at roughly 110-112°, looking properly thrown open. I'll pose the lid around its hinge joint at that angle, making sure all lid parts including the studs are built before applying the pose so they inherit the rotation correctly, and leave the padlock attached loosely to the base.

For the closed-pose geometry, I'm working out the lid's curved outline as an ellipse arc extruded with 0.9 thickness to match the body flush, then setting up the paint call for the lid surface.

I'll compute the angle from the lid's pivot to determine which plank each point belongs to, alternating between four wood grain colors with dark seams at plank boundaries, using nested grain paints that streak along the x-axis for a natural wood texture on both the surface and end caps.

For the iron hardware, I'm planning to use a mottled iron/rust color paint for the straps to give them a weathered, rusty look rather than flat metal colors.

For the interior, I'm thinking through the gap between the mound of coins and the chest walls — since the mound doesn't fully reach the corners, I need to add a filler box of gold beneath/around it so there's no visible dark gap at the bottom.

Now I'm working out the mound shape as a height function based on an elliptical falloff, and planning to scatter coins randomly across the top surface wherever they fall within that elliptical boundary.

I'm checking that the floor pile sphere doesn't sink too far below the floor plane, since the model only allows about 2% overhang—so I'm adjusting the center and radius to keep the bottom within tolerance, using a partial dome geometry (open bottom, not visible) for both the floor pile and the blob instead of a full sphere.

Now I'm writing a generic coin-scattering function that samples random directions over a sphere, maps them onto an ellipsoid surface, filters points using a normal-based test (favoring front/top-facing areas), and places each coin slightly offset along the surface normal with a random spin around that axis to vary orientation.

Writing skull and crossbones SVG...

Still working out texture placement...

Adding top bands and planning how the lid straps curve down to meet the front body straps, tracing the elliptical path endpoints for the strap geometry.

Now I'm placing the straps at x ±0.28 and figuring out the hasp plate position on the lid's front face, which is nearly vertical near the bottom edge where φ≈0 — so I'll size a small rounded box there for the plate.

Then I'm working out the matching lock plate on the base and a small torus for the staple, positioning both so the hasp mechanism reads correctly with the lid open, and sketching the shackle torus to hang through the staple.

I'll lower the lock body so the shackle arch overlaps and interlocks through the staple ring, positioning the body box to clear the skull top, then add a slight tilt rotation to make the lock look like it's hanging loose.

Setting up pivot-relative local coordinates for each lock part, computing a shared rotation about the pivot point, and defining the torus shackle arc and body box offsets accordingly.

Still positioning lid elements...

Now I'm adding the corner pieces and straps using an iron mottle texture for the metal paint, then placing decorative studs along the vertical straps as small flattened spheres bound to the box base and lid.

I'm mirroring the strap loop to cover the back side as well, placing lid straps symmetrically on both x sides, and adding end cap plates at the lid edges using a slightly enlarged extruded profile to cap off the lid body.

I'm working out the band's orientation so its thickness runs radially in-plane rather than along the x-axis, and sizing it so the strap sits close to the ellipse radius without poking out too far from the surface.

Now I'm planning the wood plank construction for the body: breaking the front wall into four horizontal planks with small gaps between them, then setting up box dimensions and positions for the front, back, and side walls around the interior cavity.

I'll skip extra scratches and nicks for simplicity, then start building the chest structure with a builder utility—setting up joints for the base and hinged lid using helper functions for geometry and positioning.

Writing wood grain and plank geometry...

Adding the dome mound and rim trim boxes now, adjusting offsets slightly to avoid z-fighting between the corner straps and trim bands.

Still adjusting plate positions...

I'm mapping how the rotated lock components fit together — the shackle as a half-torus arching into the body, with positions computed relative to the pivot so the body sits just above the skull surface without clipping. Checking that the body's back edge stays clear of the plate and confirming handle positions along x.

Writing lid strap generator function...

Placing studs and end bands now, working out tube radii and normal direction for the curved path to make sure the cross-section orients correctly along the frame.

Now I'm generating pearls along a catmull-rom path through small sphere geometries, checking the starting point sits properly outside the mound surface so nothing clips through the walls.

Still plotting pearl positions...

Now I'm placing the goblet near the coin mound and working out its lathe profile, making sure the inner and outer wall curves don't cross each other.

Placing scattered gems...

Still writing coin placement logic...

Checking whether coin positions actually sit on or inside the dome surface at various angles — the dome's horizontal radius differs from the coin ellipsoid's, so at steeper angles the dome height drops to zero while coins still try to sit at their default height, meaning I need to clamp coins to the actual dome surface rather than assume a fixed offset.

Now checking the floor pile dome placement against the chest front face - shifting its center to z=0.5 so it spans 0.3 to 0.7 without clipping into the wall, and adjusting the x range to -0.16 to 0.5. Then comparing against the blob position, centered at (0.27, 0.22, 0.33) with radii giving a z range of 0.2 to 0.46.

For the blob, I'm setting an acceptance condition favoring the upper-front area so it reads as a sloped ramp of coins, aiming for about 60 coins there, 90 in the pile, and 40 loose on the floor scattered across x 0.1-0.75 and z 0.3-0.85, keeping clear of the pearl necklace region to the left. The loose coins lie flat with slight normal jitter, and I'll skip any standing or tumbling coins to keep things simple, while making sure the chest's overall coin spread doesn't exceed x=0.75.

For the gold mound, I'm shaping a dome from a partial sphere scaled flat and wide, positioning it just above the floor, and giving it a mottled gold shading for texture. I'm also writing a paint function for the lid's wood grain, using an angle calculation from the point coordinates to generate seam lines and vary the wood color procedurally.

Now I'm defining the lid's elliptical outline by stepping through angles from one side to the other, generating 13 points, then closing the shape with a straight edge back to the starting point.

I'm setting the extrude parameters for the lid geometry—thickness, bone attachment, position, and a small bevel—and then starting on the box dimensions for the lid's interior lining piece.

Adding plane for the skull texture, merging coin geometries with a guard for null results, then setting up a seeded PRNG for deterministic randomness when placing gems with random rotations and scaling.

I'm positioning torus pieces for staple and lock shackle details, carefully working out radius, thickness, and rotation so the ring pokes partly into the plate and wall for a realistic embedded look.
